{{short description|Concept in measure theory}}
{{no footnotes|date=March 2016}}
In [[mathematics]], '''tightness''' is a concept in [[measure theory]]. The intuitive idea is that a given collection of measures does not "escape to [[infinity]]".<!-- and beyond!-->

==Definitions==

Let <math>(X, T)</math> be a [[Hausdorff space]], and let <math>\Sigma</math> be a [[sigma algebra|&sigma;-algebra]] on <math>X</math> that contains the topology <math>T</math>. (Thus, every [[open set|open subset]] of <math>X</math> is a [[measurable set]] and <math>\Sigma</math> is at least as fine as the [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel &sigma;-algebra]] on <math>X</math>.) Let <math>M</math> be a collection of (possibly [[signed measure|signed]] or [[complex measure|complex]]) measures defined on <math>\Sigma</math>. The collection <math>M</math> is called '''tight''' (or sometimes '''uniformly tight''') if, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, there is a [[compact space|compact subset]] <math>K_{\varepsilon}</math> of <math>X</math> such that, for all measures <math>\mu \in M</math>,

:<math>|\mu| (X \setminus K_{\varepsilon}) < \varepsilon.</math>

where <math>|\mu|</math> is the [[total variation measure]] of <math>\mu</math>.  Very often, the measures in question are [[probability measure]]s, so the last part can be written as

:<math>\mu (K_{\varepsilon}) > 1 - \varepsilon. \,</math>

If a tight collection <math>M</math> consists of a single measure <math>\mu</math>, then (depending upon the author) <math>\mu</math> may either be said to be a '''tight measure''' or to be an '''[[inner regular measure]]'''.

If <math>Y</math> is an <math>X</math>-valued [[random variable]] whose [[probability distribution]] on <math>X</math> is a tight measure then <math>Y</math> is said to be a '''separable random variable''' or a '''Radon random variable'''.

Another equivalent criterion of the tightness of a collection <math>M</math> is sequential weak compactness. We say the family <math>M</math> of probability measures is sequentially weakly compact if for every sequence <math>\left\{\mu_n\right\}</math> from the family, there is a subsequence of measures that converges weakly to some probability measure <math>\mu</math>. It can be shown that a family of measures is tight if and only if it is sequentially weakly compact.

==Examples==

===Compact spaces===

If <math>X</math> is a [[metrizable]] [[compact space]], then every collection of (possibly complex) measures on <math>X</math> is tight. This is not necessarily so for non-metrisable compact spaces. If we take <math>[0,\omega_1]</math> with its [[order topology]], then there exists a measure <math>\mu</math> on it that is not inner regular. Therefore, the singleton <math>\{\mu\}</math> is not tight.

===Polish spaces===

If <math>X</math> is a [[Polish space]], then every finite measure on <math>X</math> is tight; this is Ulam's theorem. Furthermore, by [[Prokhorov's theorem]], a collection of probability measures on <math>X</math> is tight if and only if
it is [[Relatively compact subspace|precompact]] in the topology of [[Convergence of measures|weak convergence]].

===A collection of point masses===

Consider the [[real line]] <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with its usual Borel topology. Let <math>\delta_{x}</math> denote the [[Dirac measure]], a unit mass at the point <math>x</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. The collection
<math display=block>M_{1} := \{ \delta_{n} \mid n \in \mathbb{N} \}</math>
is not tight, since the compact subsets of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> are precisely the [[Closed set|closed]] and [[Bounded set|bounded]] subsets, and any such set, since it is bounded, has <math>\delta_{n}</math>-measure zero for large enough <math>n</math>. On the other hand, the collection
<math display=block>M_{2} := \{ \delta_{1 / n} \mid n \in \mathbb{N} \}</math>
is tight: the compact interval <math>[0, 1]</math> will work as <math>K_{\varepsilon}</math> for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>. In general, a collection of Dirac delta measures on <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> is tight if, and only if, the collection of their [[support (measure theory)|supports]] is bounded.

===A collection of Gaussian measures===

Consider <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> with its usual Borel topology and σ-algebra. Consider a collection of [[Gaussian measure]]s
<math display=block>\Gamma = \{ \gamma_{i} \mid i \in I \},</math>
where the measure <math>\gamma_{i}</math> has [[expected value]] ([[mean]]) <math>m_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}</math> and [[covariance matrix]] <math>C_{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}</math>. Then the collection <math>\Gamma</math> is tight if, and only if, the collections <math>\{ m_{i} \mid i \in I \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n}</math> and <math>\{ C_{i} \mid i \in I \} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}</math> are both bounded.

==Tightness and convergence==

Tightness is often a necessary criterion for proving the [[weak convergence of measures|weak convergence]] of a sequence of probability measures, especially when the measure space has [[Infinity|infinite]] [[dimension]]. See

* [[Finite-dimensional distribution]]
* [[Prokhorov's theorem]]
* [[Lévy–Prokhorov metric]]
* [[Weak convergence of measures]]
* [[Classical Wiener space#Tightness in classical Wiener space|Tightness in classical Wiener space]]
* [[Càdlàg#Tightness in Skorokhod space|Tightness in Skorokhod space]]

==Tightness and stochastic ordering==

A family of real-valued random variables <math>\{X_i\}_{i \in I}</math> is tight if and only if there exists an almost surely finite random variable
<math>X</math> such that
<math> |X_i| \le_\mathrm{st} X</math> for all <math>i \in I</math>, where
<math>\le_\mathrm{st}</math> denotes the [[stochastic order]] defined by
<math>A \le_\mathrm{st} B</math> if <math>\mathbb{E}[ \phi(A)] \le \mathbb{E}[ \phi(B)]</math> for all nondecreasing functions <math>\phi</math>.
<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Leskelä, L.|author2=Vihola, M. | date=2013 |title=Stochastic order characterization of uniform integrability and tightness |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167715212003690?via%3Dihub| journal=Statistics and Probability Letters | language=en | volume=83 | issue=1 | pages=382–389 | doi=10.1016/j.spl.2012.09.023| arxiv=1106.0607 }}</ref>

==Exponential tightness==

A strengthening of tightness is the concept of exponential tightness, which has applications in [[large deviations theory]]. A family of [[probability measure]]s <math>(\mu_{\delta})_{\delta > 0}</math> on a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] topological space <math>X</math> is said to be '''exponentially tight''' if, for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, there is a compact subset <math>K_{\varepsilon}</math> of <math>X</math> such that

:<math>\limsup_{\delta \downarrow 0} \delta \log \mu_{\delta} (X \setminus K_{\varepsilon}) < - \varepsilon.</math>
